Accessible design also tends to benefit everyone: clear language, strong contrast, logical structure and forgiving interactions help people who are tired, stressed or unfamiliar with the system. When leaders insist that new technology is tested with diverse users in realistic conditions, they protect their investment and widen the group of people who can benefit from it. It also signals to staff and customers that their experience is taken seriously.

sections.heading: How Datalidy applies human-computer interaction principles
paragraphs: Datalidy's roots include university teaching in design and computing and years of practice in human-computer interaction and persuasive technology. We apply human-computer interaction principles to technology adoption challenges inside and outside organizations: customer and patient portals, digital health products, internal platforms and AI tools. We evaluate systems against established heuristics, observe people using them in context and analyze behavioral data to find where adoption stalls. We then redesign interfaces, onboarding and workflows, and test the changes before scaling them. The aim is technology that fits the people using it, so that investment translates into the behaviors that drive results. Progress is tracked through behavioral signals such as task completion, error rates and repeat use.

faqs.q: What is human-computer interaction in simple terms?
faqs.a: Human-computer interaction is the study and design of how people use technology. It looks at how people perceive, understand and operate digital systems, and how those systems can be designed to fit human abilities and goals. Its principles help explain why some technology feels intuitive while other technology causes confusion, errors and abandonment, and they guide teams in building systems people can actually use.

faqs.q: What is the difference between HCI and UX design?
faqs.a: Human-computer interaction is the broader academic and research field that studies people and technology. User experience, or UX, design is a professional practice that applies HCI principles, along with visual design, content strategy and research methods, to create specific products and services. HCI provides much of the evidence base that good UX design draws on, and the two communities overlap considerably.

faqs.q: How can leaders tell if a system has usability problems?
faqs.a: Look for indirect signals: low adoption, frequent support requests, workarounds such as parallel spreadsheets, repeated errors in the same place and complaints that the system slows people down. Then observe people using it in their real environment. Watching a few people attempt common tasks usually reveals the most important problems quickly and gives clear direction for improvement.

insights.title: Emotion and Decision-Making
insights.meta_title: Emotion and Decision-Making: How Feelings Shape Choices
insights.meta_description: How emotion and decision-making are linked, why feelings are essential to good judgment, when they mislead, and how leaders and designers can work with them.
insights.summary: Why emotion is not the enemy of good decisions, how feelings guide judgment, when they lead people astray, and what this means for leaders, customers and patients.
insights.dek: The old view held that good decisions require setting emotion aside. Modern neuroscience and psychology show the opposite: emotion is part of how people decide. The practical question is not whether feelings influence choices, but how to work with them well.
key_takeaways: Emotion is integral to decision-making; people with impaired emotional processing often struggle to make even simple choices.
Feelings act as fast signals about value and risk, which helps in familiar situations and misleads in unfamiliar ones.
Incidental emotions, such as stress or mood from unrelated events, can distort decisions without people noticing.
Leaders and designers can account for emotion through timing, framing, structured reflection and environments that reduce unnecessary stress.

sections.heading: Rethinking the role of emotion in decisions
paragraphs: For much of intellectual history, emotion and reason were treated as opponents. Good decisions, the thinking went, came from calm analysis, and feelings were noise to be suppressed. Research over recent decades has overturned that view. The relationship between emotion and decision-making is not a contest but a partnership. Emotions help people notice what matters, assign value to options and act when information is incomplete, which describes most real decisions. Without them, people can analyze endlessly yet struggle to choose. Understanding this partnership is useful for anyone who makes decisions under uncertainty or designs choices for others, from executives and investors to clinicians, product teams and public health communicators.

This does not mean feelings are always right. Emotions evolved to help people respond quickly to recurring situations, and they can be badly calibrated for modern ones. Anxiety can magnify a small risk; excitement can hide a large one. The goal is not to remove emotion from decisions, which is impossible, but to understand which emotional signals are informative and which are distortions. Leaders who grasp this can make better decisions themselves, create conditions for better decisions in their teams and design products, services and messages that respect how customers and patients actually choose.

sections.heading: The somatic marker hypothesis
paragraphs: One of the most influential accounts of emotion and decision-making comes from neuroscientist Antonio Damasio. Studying patients with damage to parts of the prefrontal cortex involved in processing emotion, he observed that many retained their intelligence and reasoning abilities yet made poor personal and professional decisions. Some struggled to make simple choices at all, weighing options endlessly. Damasio proposed the somatic marker hypothesis: through experience, people learn to associate situations and options with bodily feelings, such as unease or attraction. These markers act as rapid signals that narrow the field of options and guide choice before conscious analysis is complete. When the markers are missing, decision-making becomes slow, unanchored and often unwise.

The hypothesis has been debated and refined, and not every detail has held up, but its central insight is widely accepted: emotional signals are part of the machinery of judgment, not an interference with it. This connects to research on expert intuition, where experienced professionals report a feeling that something is wrong before they can explain why. Those feelings often encode real patterns learned through experience. The implication for leaders is to treat gut feelings as data, worth noticing and examining, rather than either obeying them blindly or dismissing them as irrational.

sections.heading: When emotions help and when they mislead
paragraphs: Emotions are most helpful when they are integral to the decision, meaning they arise from the situation itself and reflect relevant experience. Unease about a deal that seems too good, or confidence about a familiar operational call, can carry genuine information. Emotions are most misleading when they are incidental, arising from something unrelated to the decision. Research shows that mood from an unrelated event, fatigue, stress or even the weather can shift risk tolerance and judgments without people realizing it. Several patterns are worth recognizing, because each suggests a specific safeguard that individuals and teams can adopt.
bullets: Affect heuristic: people judge risks and benefits by how an option makes them feel overall.
Loss aversion: the pain of losing tends to outweigh the pleasure of an equivalent gain.
Stress narrowing: acute stress shrinks attention and pushes people toward habitual responses.
Mood carryover: emotions from one situation spill into unrelated decisions that follow.
Projection: people underestimate how differently they will feel in a future emotional state.

sections.heading: Emotion and decision-making in organizations
paragraphs: Inside organizations, emotion shapes decisions at every level. Executives under pressure may become more risk averse or more impulsive, depending on temperament and context. Teams in a climate of fear tend to suppress bad news, so leaders decide with incomplete information. Anxiety around a reorganization can make people resist changes they would otherwise support. Leaders can account for this by building routines that create space between feeling and action: pausing before major decisions, separating the meeting where options are generated from the meeting where they are chosen, asking how a decision would look from a calmer vantage point and inviting dissent explicitly. These practices do not remove emotion. They let it inform rather than dominate.

Outside organizations, emotion and decision-making shape how customers, patients and community members respond. A patient anxious about a diagnosis may struggle to absorb treatment instructions, however clear. A borrower stressed about finances may avoid opening statements that would help them. A customer excited about a purchase may overlook terms they will later regret. Designing for these realities means timing information for moments when people can use it, reducing unnecessary stress in processes and interfaces, framing choices honestly and offering support at emotionally difficult points. Ethical design works with emotion to help people act on their own considered goals, never to exploit moments of vulnerability.

sections.heading: How Datalidy applies emotion and decision-making research
paragraphs: Datalidy's foundation in clinical and health psychology and behavioral medicine shapes how we approach emotion and decision-making. With leaders, we use executive coaching to help them recognize their own emotional patterns under pressure and build routines that keep judgment sound. With teams, we design decision processes that surface dissent and reduce the distortions of stress and fear. In customer, patient and member experiences, we map the emotional journey alongside the behavioral one, identify the moments where anxiety, confusion or overconfidence derail good choices, and design and test changes that help people decide in their own interest. Throughout, we treat emotional signals as data worth understanding rather than noise to be ignored.

faqs.q: Do emotions make decisions worse?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Emotions are an essential part of how people evaluate options and act under uncertainty. People with impaired emotional processing often struggle to decide at all. Emotions become a problem when they are incidental to the decision, such as stress from an unrelated event, or when they are poorly calibrated to an unfamiliar situation. The aim is to understand emotional signals, not to eliminate them.

faqs.q: What is the somatic marker hypothesis?
faqs.a: The somatic marker hypothesis, proposed by neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, suggests that people learn to associate situations and options with bodily feelings through experience. These feelings, or markers, act as fast signals that guide choices before conscious reasoning is complete. The idea emerged from studies of patients whose emotional processing was impaired and who, despite intact reasoning, often made poor decisions in their personal and professional lives.

faqs.q: How can leaders manage emotion in high-stakes decisions?
faqs.a: Build routines that create space between feeling and action. Pause before irreversible choices, separate option generation from selection, invite dissent explicitly and ask how the decision would look under calmer conditions. Notice incidental stress or fatigue and, where possible, avoid making major decisions in those states. Coaching can help leaders recognize their personal patterns and develop habits that keep emotional signals informative rather than overwhelming.

insights.title: Psychometrics for Business Surveys
insights.meta_title: Psychometrics for Business Surveys: Reliability and Validity
insights.meta_description: How psychometrics improves business surveys through reliability, validity, item design and scale construction, so surveys measure what they claim to measure.
insights.summary: How the science of psychological measurement makes business surveys trustworthy, from reliability and validity to item writing, scale design and connecting survey scores to behavior.
insights.dek: Organizations run engagement surveys, customer surveys and culture assessments constantly, then make decisions based on the scores. Psychometrics asks whether those scores deserve that trust. Applying its principles turns surveys from opinion snapshots into reliable measurement.
key_takeaways: Psychometrics is the science of measuring psychological attributes, and it applies directly to engagement, customer and culture surveys.
Reliability asks whether a measure is consistent; validity asks whether it measures what it claims to measure.
Poorly written items, such as double-barreled or leading questions, introduce error that no amount of analysis can remove.
The most useful surveys are validated against behavior, showing that scores actually predict outcomes leaders care about.

sections.heading: What psychometrics is and why it matters for business
paragraphs: Psychometrics is the science of measuring psychological attributes such as attitudes, abilities, personality traits and experiences. It developed alongside psychological testing and now underpins assessments used in education, clinical practice and research. Its core concern is simple: when a number is assigned to something that cannot be observed directly, such as engagement, trust or satisfaction, how confident can anyone be that the number means what it appears to mean? Business surveys face exactly this problem. Employee engagement, customer satisfaction, psychological safety, brand perception and leadership effectiveness are all psychological constructs. Psychometrics provides the tools to measure them well.

Many business surveys are built without these tools. Questions are drafted by committee, revised for tone and launched without testing. The resulting scores are reported to two decimal places, tracked over time and used to evaluate managers or set strategy. If the underlying measure is unreliable or invalid, these decisions rest on noise. Changes from one quarter to the next may reflect question wording, sampling or chance rather than real change. Applying basic psychometric discipline does not require turning every survey into a research project. It requires a few careful steps that dramatically improve the quality of the information leaders receive.

sections.heading: Reliability: is the measure consistent?
paragraphs: Reliability refers to the consistency of a measure. A reliable survey produces similar results when the underlying attribute has not changed, and its items work together to measure the same thing. Several forms of reliability are relevant to business surveys. Internal consistency asks whether items intended to measure one construct are correlated with each other, often summarized with a statistic such as Cronbach's alpha. Test-retest reliability asks whether scores are stable over a short interval when nothing has changed. Inter-rater reliability matters when people score open-ended responses or observations. Low reliability means scores contain a large share of random error, so apparent differences between teams or time periods may not be real.

Single-item measures deserve particular caution. Many dashboards rely on one question to represent a complex construct, such as a single satisfaction rating or a single likelihood-to-recommend item. Single items can be useful for quick tracking, but their reliability is difficult to assess and usually lower than that of a well-designed multi-item scale. When decisions with real consequences depend on a score, such as manager evaluations or investment in a program, a short multi-item scale with demonstrated reliability is a far safer foundation than a lone question, however familiar it has become.

sections.heading: Validity: does it measure what it claims?
paragraphs: A measure can be perfectly consistent and still measure the wrong thing. Validity addresses whether a survey actually captures the construct it is intended to capture and supports the decisions made with it. Modern psychometrics treats validity as an accumulation of evidence rather than a single test. For business surveys, several kinds of evidence are especially useful, and leaders can ask for each of them before relying on survey results for important decisions.
bullets: Content validity: the items cover the full scope of the construct, not just part of it.
Construct validity: the items group together in the expected pattern and relate sensibly to other measures.
Convergent validity: scores correlate with other measures of the same or similar constructs.
Discriminant validity: scores are distinguishable from measures of different constructs.
Predictive validity: scores forecast relevant future behavior, such as retention, adoption or purchase.
Fairness: items work similarly across groups, without systematic bias.

sections.heading: Writing better survey items
paragraphs: Even a well-planned survey can be undermined by poorly written items, because every flaw in wording adds error that analysis cannot remove. Common problems include double-barreled questions that ask about two things at once, such as satisfaction with pay and benefits; leading questions that signal a preferred answer; vague terms that respondents interpret differently; jargon unfamiliar to respondents; and response scales that are unbalanced or poorly labeled. Good practice includes using plain language, asking about one idea per item, anchoring scales clearly, including a mix of positively and negatively framed items where appropriate and pilot testing with a small group before launch. Cognitive interviews, in which respondents explain how they interpret each question, often reveal surprising misunderstandings.

Survey design also affects who responds and how. Long surveys produce fatigue and careless answers toward the end. Surveys perceived as unsafe produce socially desirable answers rather than honest ones, which is especially important for engagement and culture measures. Response rates that vary widely across groups can distort comparisons. Thoughtful design addresses these issues by keeping surveys focused, explaining how data will be used and protected, and analyzing who did and did not respond before drawing conclusions.

sections.heading: How Datalidy applies psychometrics to business surveys
paragraphs: Datalidy's background in research methods, test and measurement and psychometrics informs every survey we design or evaluate. We audit existing engagement, customer, patient and culture surveys for reliability and validity, identify items that add noise and recommend focused improvements. When building new instruments, we define constructs clearly, write and pilot items, test reliability and examine structure before launch. Most importantly, we connect survey measures to behavioral signals, testing whether scores predict outcomes such as retention, adoption, adherence or performance. That link turns surveys from descriptive snapshots into predictive KPIs that leaders can act on with confidence.

We also help organizations use survey results responsibly. That means reporting scores with appropriate context, such as response rates and the range of normal variation, so that small movements are not mistaken for real change. It means protecting confidentiality so that people continue to answer honestly. And it means closing the loop with respondents by sharing what was learned and what will change, which sustains participation and trust over time. Good measurement is not only a technical achievement. It is a relationship with the people being measured, and it works best when they can see that their answers lead to action.

faqs.q: What is the difference between reliability and validity?
faqs.a: Reliability is about consistency: whether a measure produces stable results and whether its items work together. Validity is about meaning: whether the measure actually captures the intended construct and supports the decisions made with it. A measure can be reliable without being valid, consistently measuring the wrong thing, but it cannot be valid without being reasonably reliable, because random error undermines any meaningful interpretation.

faqs.q: Are single-question surveys useful?
faqs.a: Single-question measures can be useful for quick, frequent tracking where a rough signal is enough. Their limitations are that reliability is hard to establish and a single item rarely captures a complex construct fully. When scores drive important decisions, such as evaluating managers or investing in programs, a short multi-item scale with demonstrated reliability and validity provides a much stronger basis for action.

faqs.q: How do you validate a business survey?
faqs.a: Start by defining the construct clearly and checking that items cover it fully. Pilot the survey, test internal consistency and examine whether items group as expected. Compare scores with other relevant measures to establish convergent and discriminant validity. Most valuable for business purposes is predictive validity: testing whether scores forecast meaningful behavior, such as retention, purchase or adoption, over time.

insights.title: Data Visualization for Better Decisions
insights.meta_description: How data visualization supports better decisions: perception research, chart choice, dashboard design and habits that help leaders see signal, not noise.
insights.summary: How perception research and design principles turn charts and dashboards into decision tools, so leaders see the signals that matter instead of drowning in metrics.
insights.dek: Most dashboards are built to display data, not to support decisions. The difference matters. Data visualization for decision-making starts with the decision, uses what is known about human perception and puts the most predictive signals where leaders will see them first.
key_takeaways: Effective visualization starts with the decision a leader needs to make, not with the data that happens to be available.
Perception research shows that people judge position and length far more accurately than angle, area or color intensity.
Removing visual clutter and showing comparisons, trends and uncertainty helps leaders separate real signals from noise.
The best dashboards lead with a few predictive, behavior-based KPIs rather than dozens of lagging metrics.

sections.heading: From displaying data to supporting decisions
paragraphs: Organizations have never had more data or more dashboards. Yet leaders frequently report that they still struggle to know what is happening and what to do about it. The problem is rarely a lack of information. It is that visualizations are built to display what is available rather than to answer the questions that drive decisions. Data visualization for decision-making reverses the process. It begins by asking who will use the visualization, what decision they need to make, how often and under what conditions. Only then does it ask which data and which visual forms will make the relevant signal obvious. This shift sounds modest but changes almost every design choice that follows.

A decision-centered approach also clarifies what to leave out. A dashboard showing fifty metrics treats them all as equally important, which forces the viewer to do the work of prioritizing every time. A dashboard built around a handful of leading indicators, with supporting detail available on demand, does that work in advance. It reflects a judgment about what matters, which is exactly the judgment leaders need help making. The best visualizations are therefore not neutral. They embody a theory of what drives results and invite the viewer to test it.

sections.heading: What perception research tells us
paragraphs: Good data visualization rests on how human vision and cognition actually work. In foundational research, statisticians William Cleveland and Robert McGill studied how accurately people decode different visual encodings. They found that people judge position along a common scale most accurately, followed by length, with angle, area, volume and color intensity progressively harder to read precisely. This is why bar charts and dot plots usually communicate comparisons better than pie charts or bubble charts, and why three-dimensional effects tend to distort perception. Edward Tufte, through his influential books, argued for maximizing the share of ink devoted to data, removing decoration that does not inform, and showing comparisons clearly. Together these ideas form a practical toolkit.
bullets: Use position and length for the comparisons that matter most.
Avoid three-dimensional effects, which distort size and position.
Remove gridlines, borders and decoration that do not carry information.
Use color sparingly and purposefully, to highlight rather than decorate.
Label data directly where possible, rather than relying on separate legends.
Use small multiples to compare many groups on a consistent scale.

sections.heading: Separating signal from noise
paragraphs: Many poor decisions stem from reacting to noise as if it were signal. A metric moves up one week and down the next, and leaders respond to each movement with praise, concern or a new initiative. Most of these fluctuations are ordinary variation. Visualizations can help by showing data in context: longer time series rather than single comparisons, reference lines for targets or historical ranges, and clear indications of uncertainty where estimates are involved. Techniques from statistical process control, such as control charts, help distinguish routine variation from genuine shifts. Showing sample sizes alongside rates prevents overreacting to small groups. These choices make a dashboard slightly more complex but far more honest.

Context also includes the behaviors behind the numbers. A revenue chart tells leaders what happened; it rarely tells them why or what will happen next. Pairing outcome metrics with the behavioral indicators that predict them, such as activation, engagement or adherence, gives leaders time to act before results arrive. Visual design can reinforce this relationship by placing leading indicators first and showing how they connect to lagging outcomes. When leaders can see the chain from behavior to result, conversations shift from explaining last quarter to influencing next quarter, which is where decisions can still change the result.

sections.heading: Designing dashboards people actually use
paragraphs: A dashboard is a product, and it succeeds or fails on the same terms as any other product: whether its intended users find it useful enough to return to. Many dashboards are abandoned because they were designed without observing how leaders actually make decisions. Principles from human-computer interaction apply directly here. Know the users and their tasks. Test early prototypes with them. Use consistent layouts so people learn where to look. Make the most important information visible at a glance and detail available on demand. Keep definitions clear and accessible so that numbers are interpreted consistently. Finally, revisit dashboards regularly, retiring metrics that no longer inform decisions and adding those that do.

Accessibility and context of use matter too. Visualizations should work for people with color vision deficiencies, which means not relying on red and green alone to carry meaning. They should be legible on the devices where decisions are actually made, which increasingly includes phones. And they should be accompanied by enough narrative to guide interpretation, whether through annotations, short summaries or regular review conversations where teams discuss what the data shows and what they will do about it. Visualization is most valuable as the start of a conversation, not the end of one.

sections.heading: How Datalidy approaches data visualization for decision-making
paragraphs: Datalidy combines behavioral data analysis, human-computer interaction and decision science in its data visualization and decision dashboard work. We start by understanding the decisions leaders face and observing how they currently use data. Using Behavioral Signals Design, we identify the predictive, behavior-based KPIs that should sit at the center of the view. We then design visualizations grounded in perception research, test them with the people who will use them and refine until the signal is clear. The result is a small number of decision-focused dashboards that help leaders see what is changing, why and what to do next. We also help teams build review routines around those dashboards, so that the data is discussed, questioned and acted on rather than simply displayed.

faqs.q: What makes a good dashboard?
faqs.a: A good dashboard is built around specific decisions and users. It leads with a few meaningful indicators, ideally including leading measures that predict outcomes, and makes detail available on demand. It uses chart types that people read accurately, avoids clutter, shows trends and context rather than isolated numbers, and keeps definitions clear. Above all, it is used regularly because people find it genuinely helpful.

faqs.q: Why are pie charts often discouraged?
faqs.a: Perception research shows that people compare angles and areas less accurately than positions and lengths. With more than a few slices, or slices of similar size, pie charts make comparisons difficult. Bar charts or dot plots usually communicate the same information more clearly. Pie charts can still work for showing a simple part-to-whole relationship with two or three categories, but they are rarely the best option.

faqs.q: How many metrics should an executive dashboard include?
faqs.a: There is no fixed number, but fewer is usually better. An executive dashboard should highlight the handful of indicators most closely tied to the decisions leaders make, with supporting metrics available through drill-down. If every metric appears with equal prominence, leaders must prioritize on the fly, which defeats the purpose. Focus on measures that predict outcomes, not just those that report them.

insights.title: Systems Thinking for Leaders
insights.meta_title: Systems Thinking for Leaders: A Practical Introduction
insights.meta_description: Systems thinking for leaders: feedback loops, delays, leverage points and unintended consequences, and how to use them to solve problems that keep coming back.
insights.summary: A practical introduction to systems thinking for leaders: feedback loops, delays, stocks and flows, and where to intervene so that problems stay solved instead of returning.
insights.dek: Some problems refuse to stay fixed. Every intervention seems to work briefly, then the problem returns or reappears somewhere else. Systems thinking explains why, and gives leaders practical tools for finding interventions that hold.
key_takeaways: Systems thinking looks at how parts of an organization interact over time, rather than treating problems as isolated events.
Feedback loops, delays and accumulations explain why well-intended fixes often backfire or produce only temporary relief.
Donella Meadows showed that the most powerful interventions change goals, rules and information flows, not just numbers.
Behavior is where systems become visible; mapping behavioral feedback loops reveals where change will actually hold.

sections.heading: What systems thinking is
paragraphs: Systems thinking is a way of understanding how the parts of a complex whole interact to produce its behavior over time. Instead of asking what caused a single event, it asks what structure keeps producing a pattern of events. An organization, a market, a health system and a community are all systems: collections of people, processes, incentives and information connected by relationships that shape what each part does. When leaders view a problem as a system, they stop searching for one cause or one culprit and start looking for the feedback loops, delays and incentives that make the problem persistent. This shift is especially useful for problems that keep returning despite repeated efforts to solve them.

Systems thinking for leaders is not an abstract philosophy. It is a practical discipline with tools that can be applied in a workshop or a strategy meeting. Causal loop diagrams show how variables reinforce or balance each other. Stock-and-flow maps show what accumulates and what drains away over time. Behavior-over-time graphs show how key measures have actually moved, revealing patterns that single data points hide. Used together, these tools help leadership teams build a shared picture of how their organization really works, which is often quite different from the picture on the organizational chart or in the strategic plan.

sections.heading: Core concepts every leader should know
paragraphs: A small vocabulary does most of the work in systems thinking. Once leaders recognize these concepts, they begin to see them everywhere: in sales cycles, hiring pipelines, customer churn, staff burnout and the spread of new practices. The concepts are simple to state but powerful in combination, because most real organizational problems involve several of them interacting at once. Learning to spot them is the first practical step toward intervening well.
bullets: Stocks and flows: quantities that accumulate, such as talent or trust, and the rates that change them.
Reinforcing loops: cycles that amplify change, driving growth or decline.
Balancing loops: cycles that resist change and push the system toward a goal or limit.
Delays: lags between action and effect that cause overreaction and oscillation.
Boundaries: choices about what is inside the system, which determine what leaders can see.
Unintended consequences: effects that emerge elsewhere in the system, often after a delay.

sections.heading: Why quick fixes often backfire
paragraphs: Systems thinkers have identified recurring patterns, sometimes called archetypes, that explain why sensible interventions fail. In one common pattern, a quick fix relieves a symptom while weakening the system's ability to address the underlying cause. Hiring contractors to cover chronic overload, for example, eases pressure today but delays the structural changes that would reduce overload permanently. In another, a successful initiative grows until it hits a limit nobody was watching, such as a sales push that outpaces the service team's capacity, and performance declines. In a third, two parts of the organization each pursue their own goals in ways that undercut the other, escalating effort without improving results.

Delays make all of these patterns harder to see. When the effect of an action appears months later, leaders often misattribute it, or abandon a sound strategy before it has time to work, or double down on a poor one because the costs have not yet arrived. Behavioral programs are especially vulnerable. A new onboarding experience may improve retention only after several months. A culture initiative may produce early enthusiasm that fades before habits form. Recognizing the role of delays encourages patience where it is warranted and earlier measurement of leading indicators, so leaders know whether a change is on track long before the lagging result appears.

sections.heading: Finding leverage points
paragraphs: Donella Meadows, one of the most influential systems thinkers, described leverage points as places in a system where a small shift can produce large changes in behavior. She ranked them from least to most powerful. Adjusting parameters such as budgets, targets and headcounts is the most common intervention and often the least effective, because the system's structure tends to absorb the change. More powerful are changes to feedback loops, especially adding or strengthening information flows so that people can see the consequences of their actions sooner. More powerful still are changes to the rules of the system, its goals and the mindset from which it arises. These deeper interventions are harder to make but far more durable.

For leaders, this ranking offers a useful discipline. Before adding another target or incentive, ask whether the people involved can actually see how their behavior affects outcomes. Many organizational problems persist because feedback is slow, aggregated or delivered to the wrong people. Giving a frontline team timely visibility into the customer behaviors their work influences can change practice more than a new bonus scheme. Clarifying what the organization is really optimizing for, and whether stated goals match the goals rewarded in practice, often reveals why behavior has drifted away from strategy and what needs to change for it to return.

sections.heading: How Datalidy applies systems thinking
paragraphs: Datalidy uses systems thinking for leaders as a practical lens across its work. Behavior is where systems become visible: every feedback loop, delay and incentive shows up in what people actually do. In Behavioral Signals Design, we map the full journey and the data around it, often across systems that were never integrated, and identify the behavioral loops that drive outcomes. We work with leadership teams to build shared maps of their organization's dynamics, find leverage points and design interventions that strengthen feedback rather than simply adjusting targets. We then test those interventions and track leading indicators, so leaders can see whether the system is changing well before the lagging results arrive.

faqs.q: What is systems thinking in simple terms?
faqs.a: Systems thinking is a way of understanding problems by looking at how the parts of a situation interact over time, rather than focusing on single causes or events. It pays attention to feedback loops, delays and accumulations that keep producing the same patterns. It helps leaders see why some problems keep returning and where to intervene so that improvements last instead of fading.

faqs.q: What is a leverage point?
faqs.a: A leverage point is a place in a system where a relatively small change can produce a large and lasting shift in behavior. Donella Meadows argued that the most powerful leverage points are not budgets or targets but information flows, rules, goals and underlying mindsets. In organizations, improving how quickly people see the consequences of their actions is often a strong and underused leverage point.

faqs.q: How can leaders start using systems thinking?
faqs.a: Begin with a persistent problem and plot how key measures have changed over time. Then map, with the people involved, the factors that influence those measures and how they connect, looking for reinforcing and balancing loops and delays. Ask what the system is actually rewarding. Even a simple shared map often reveals why past fixes failed and suggests more durable interventions.

insights.title: Closing the Research-to-Practice Gap
insights.meta_description: Why evidence takes so long to reach practice, what knowledge translation involves, and how to close the research-to-practice gap with behavioral design.
insights.summary: Why good evidence so often fails to change real-world practice, and how knowledge translation, behavioral design and implementation science can close the research-to-practice gap.
insights.dek: Research produces a steady stream of findings that could improve health, education and organizational life. Much of it never changes what people do. The research-to-practice gap is fundamentally a behavior problem, and it can be addressed with behavioral methods.
key_takeaways: The research-to-practice gap describes the long, uneven path from published evidence to routine use in real settings.
Publishing findings is rarely enough; practitioners need evidence that is accessible, relevant, trusted and easy to apply.
Knowledge translation and implementation science treat adoption of evidence as a behavior that can be designed and measured.
Organizations close the gap by co-designing with practitioners, adapting to context and tracking behavioral adoption, not just dissemination.

sections.heading: What the research-to-practice gap is
paragraphs: The research-to-practice gap is the distance between what research shows to be effective and what actually happens in clinics, classrooms, workplaces and communities. It is widely discussed in medicine, where proven treatments and practices can take many years to become standard care, but it exists in every field that produces evidence. Education research identifies teaching methods that are rarely adopted. Organizational research identifies management practices that leaders seldom use. Public health research identifies interventions that never reach the communities that need them. In each case, valuable knowledge exists, often funded with public money, yet the people who could benefit from it do not, because the evidence never becomes routine behavior.

The gap matters for reasons beyond efficiency. When effective practices are slow to spread, people receive less effective care, education or support than they could. When ineffective practices persist despite evidence against them, resources are wasted and harm can continue. The gap also tends to widen inequities, since well-resourced institutions adopt new evidence faster than under-resourced ones. For research funders, universities, associations and health systems, closing the research-to-practice gap is central to their mission. It is the difference between knowledge that exists and knowledge that changes lives.

sections.heading: Why evidence does not spread on its own
paragraphs: The traditional model of dissemination assumes that publishing findings, presenting them at conferences and issuing guidelines will lead practitioners to adopt them. Experience shows this assumption is weak. Practitioners face real barriers that publication does not address, and many of those barriers are behavioral rather than informational. Understanding them is the first step toward designing more effective translation, because each barrier points toward a different remedy. Most can be addressed by design once they are named.
bullets: Access: research is often behind paywalls or written for other researchers, not practitioners.
Relevance: studies may not reflect the populations, resources or constraints of real settings.
Trust: practitioners weigh evidence against experience and the views of respected peers.
Effort: adopting a new practice requires time, training and changes to established routines.
Context: organizational systems, incentives and workflows may not support the new behavior.
Feedback: practitioners rarely see whether changing practice actually improves outcomes.

sections.heading: Knowledge translation and implementation science
paragraphs: Two related fields have developed to address the gap systematically. Knowledge translation focuses on synthesizing, adapting and communicating research so that it can be used by practitioners, policymakers and the public. It emphasizes plain language, relevance to real decisions and engagement with the people who will use the knowledge, ideally from the start of the research rather than after it is finished. Implementation science studies the methods that promote uptake of evidence-based practices in real settings. It examines the factors that influence adoption, such as characteristics of the intervention, the setting and the people involved, and tests strategies to improve it, including training, audit and feedback, practice facilitation and changes to workflow.

Both fields recognize, implicitly or explicitly, that adopting evidence is a behavior. A clinician following a new protocol, a teacher using a new method or a manager applying a new practice must be motivated, able and prompted to act, in the language of the Fogg Behavior Model. Behavioral design adds practical methods to these fields: making the new practice as simple as possible, embedding prompts in existing workflows, using trusted messengers and social norms, and creating feedback that shows practitioners the effects of their changes. Treating translation as behavior change, rather than as information delivery, consistently produces stronger results than dissemination alone.

sections.heading: Practical ways to close the research-to-practice gap
paragraphs: Organizations that close the gap effectively share several habits. They involve practitioners early, co-designing interventions and translation materials so that evidence fits real constraints. They adapt evidence to context thoughtfully, distinguishing the core elements that make an intervention work from the peripheral details that can change. They make evidence accessible in formats practitioners actually use: brief summaries, decision aids, checklists, short videos and tools embedded in existing systems. They identify and support local champions who can model the new practice. And they measure adoption directly, tracking whether behavior changes in practice rather than counting downloads, attendance or awareness, which say little about whether anything changed.

Communication design matters throughout. Accessible scientific writing, clear visualizations and evidence-based health communication principles help findings reach practitioners and the public without distortion. This is especially important for associations, journals and research institutions whose missions depend on knowledge reaching the field. Increasingly, it also means considering how evidence will be found and summarized by search engines and AI systems, which now mediate much of how practitioners and the public encounter research. Clear, well-structured, openly available summaries are more likely to be represented accurately wherever people look for answers.

sections.heading: How Datalidy helps close the research-to-practice gap
paragraphs: Datalidy connects theory with measurable, real-world outcomes. Our research translation and knowledge dissemination work draws on university teaching, research methods, behavioral medicine and behavioral design. We help researchers, associations, health systems and funders identify the behaviors that adoption requires, understand the barriers practitioners face and design translation strategies that address them. We create accessible summaries and tools, design implementation supports such as prompts, workflows and feedback, and measure adoption through behavioral signals rather than reach alone. We also run workshops that build these skills inside organizations, so that closing the research-to-practice gap becomes a lasting capability rather than a one-time project.

This work reflects the firm's commitment to accessible scientific knowledge and to the social good that research is meant to serve. Evidence that stays in journals helps no one. Evidence that reaches a nurse at the bedside, a teacher planning a lesson or a community health worker visiting a family can change outcomes for real people. We design for that final step, measuring success by whether practice actually changes and whether the people it is meant to help are better served as a result.

faqs.q: What is knowledge translation?
faqs.a: Knowledge translation is the process of synthesizing, adapting, sharing and applying research so that it can be used by practitioners, policymakers and the public. It goes beyond publication to make evidence accessible, relevant and actionable. Good knowledge translation involves the people who will use the evidence, often from the start of a research project, and pays attention to the real contexts in which they work.

faqs.q: How is implementation science different from knowledge translation?
faqs.a: Knowledge translation focuses broadly on moving research into use, including how findings are synthesized and communicated. Implementation science is a research field that studies the methods and strategies that promote the uptake of evidence-based practices in real settings, testing which approaches actually change practice. The two overlap considerably, and many organizations draw on both when designing programs to close the research-to-practice gap.

faqs.q: How do you measure whether research has been adopted?
faqs.a: Measure behavior in practice, not just dissemination. Downloads, attendance and awareness indicate reach but not adoption. Better measures track whether practitioners actually use the new practice, how consistently and with what fidelity, and whether outcomes change as a result. These measures can come from records, observation, brief surveys or system data, and should be reviewed regularly so implementation strategies can be adjusted.

insights.title: AI, Training Data and the Cultures We Leave Behind
insights.meta_title: AI and Organizational Culture: What Your Data Teaches AI
insights.meta_description: How AI systems learn from the documents, decisions and habits organizations leave behind, and what leaders should do so AI reflects the culture they intend.
insights.summary: AI systems learn from the records organizations and cultures leave behind. What that means for bias, knowledge and values, and how leaders can shape what AI inherits.
insights.dek: Every organization leaves a trail of documents, decisions, messages and data. AI systems increasingly learn from that trail. The result is that AI inherits a culture's habits, including the ones nobody would choose to write down, unless leaders act deliberately.
key_takeaways: AI systems learn patterns from the text, records and decisions people leave behind, so they absorb culture along with content.
What an organization documents is not the same as what it values; AI learns from the record, not the intention.
AI outputs increasingly become new organizational records, creating feedback loops that can reinforce old patterns over time.
Leaders should curate the material AI learns from, make tacit values explicit and measure AI's effect on real behavior.

sections.heading: How AI learns from what cultures leave behind
paragraphs: Modern AI systems, especially large language models, learn by finding patterns in enormous collections of human-created material: books, articles, websites, forums, code and other text. They do not learn facts in isolation. They learn how people write, argue, explain, decide and relate to each other, which means they absorb the habits, assumptions and blind spots embedded in that material. In a real sense, they learn from the cultures that produced the data. When an organization then adapts an AI system to its own work, through fine-tuning on internal documents or by connecting it to a knowledge base it can search, the same principle applies at a smaller scale. The relationship between AI and organizational culture begins with this simple fact: AI reflects the record it is given.

That record is the residue of culture. Policies, emails, meeting notes, support tickets, performance reviews, sales scripts, code comments and past decisions all carry traces of how an organization actually works. Some traces are deliberate, such as written values and procedures. Many are not: the tone of internal messages, the kinds of customers who received extra attention, the questions that were never asked, the problems that were quietly worked around. An AI system trained or grounded on this material will reproduce its patterns faithfully, including the patterns leaders would not choose to repeat if they saw them clearly.

sections.heading: The record is not the culture
paragraphs: A central challenge is that what organizations write down differs from what they actually value and do. Much of any culture is tacit: carried in judgment, relationships and unwritten norms that experienced people understand but rarely document. Experts know which rules can bend, which customers need a different approach, and when the official process does not fit the situation. That knowledge seldom appears in the material AI learns from. Meanwhile, the written record overrepresents certain voices, such as those who write the most, and certain moments, such as formal decisions, while underrepresenting others. The result is an AI that knows the official version of the organization and the loudest version of its culture, but not necessarily the best one.

This gap creates predictable risks. AI may reproduce historical biases in hiring, lending, service or care, because past decisions encoded them. It may present outdated policies with confidence, because older documents outnumber newer ones. It may adopt a tone that conflicts with the culture leaders are trying to build. It may also miss the judgment calls that make experienced staff effective. None of these failures is a malfunction in the technical sense. The system is doing exactly what it was designed to do: learning from the record it was given.
bullets: Historical bias: past decisions carry patterns that may be unfair or no longer appropriate.
Stale knowledge: older material can outweigh newer guidance in what the system retrieves.
Missing tacit knowledge: expert judgment rarely appears in documents AI can learn from.
Skewed voices: the most prolific writers shape the record more than others.

sections.heading: Feedback loops: when AI output becomes the record
paragraphs: A newer dynamic deserves attention. As organizations use AI to draft emails, summarize meetings, write documentation and respond to customers, AI-generated content becomes a growing share of the organizational record. That record, in turn, may be used to train or ground future AI systems. In systems thinking terms, this is a reinforcing loop. If the AI's output reflects a narrow or outdated pattern, and that output becomes the source material for the next round, the pattern can strengthen over time without anyone deciding it should. Researchers have raised similar concerns at the scale of the public internet, where an increasing share of text is machine-generated and future models may learn partly from the output of earlier ones.

The same loop affects culture more directly. When people use AI to write, they often accept its phrasing, structure and framing, especially under time pressure. Over time, the organization's voice can drift toward the AI's defaults. Decisions supported by AI summaries may inherit what the summaries emphasized and omitted. This is not necessarily bad, since well-designed AI can raise the clarity and consistency of communication. But it means AI shapes culture as well as reflecting it, and leaders should treat that influence as something to manage deliberately rather than notice after the fact.

sections.heading: What leaders should do
paragraphs: Leaders cannot inspect every pattern an AI system has learned, but they can shape the conditions under which it learns and operates. The most effective steps are less technical than they might appear. They involve deciding what the organization wants AI to inherit, curating material accordingly, and watching how AI changes the behavior of the people and customers who use it. Responsible AI adoption is ultimately a leadership and behavior question as much as a technology question, and it belongs on the leadership agenda alongside strategy and culture.
bullets: Audit the corpus: understand which documents and data an AI system will learn from or retrieve.
Curate deliberately: retire outdated material and prioritize current, accurate, representative sources.
Make tacit knowledge explicit: capture expert judgment and values in clear, usable form.
Keep humans accountable: define where people must review, decide and own outcomes.
Test for bias: check outputs across groups and scenarios before and after deployment.
Measure behavior: track how AI changes what employees, customers and patients actually do.
Watch the loop: label AI-generated content and consider its role in future training material.

sections.heading: Culture beyond the organization
paragraphs: The same principle extends beyond any single organization. Public AI systems learn from what fields, professions and communities have published. If accurate, accessible explanations of a topic are scarce online while misleading ones are plentiful, AI systems are more likely to repeat the misleading version. For health systems, associations, research institutions and mission-driven organizations, this creates a new responsibility and a new opportunity. Publishing clear, well-structured, evidence-based material is no longer only a matter of reaching human readers directly. It also influences how AI systems describe a field to the many people who now ask them questions first, before they ever reach a professional, a website or a journal.

sections.heading: How Datalidy approaches AI and organizational culture
paragraphs: Datalidy approaches AI and organizational culture as a behavioral question. Through our responsible AI adoption work, we help leaders understand what material their AI systems learn from, where that material diverges from the culture they intend, and how to curate and supplement it. We draw on interviews and observation to capture tacit expertise, and on human-computer interaction and persuasive technology research to design AI tools that support good judgment rather than replace it. We measure adoption and impact through behavioral signals, not just usage counts. And because we care about the ethical use of persuasion and AI, we help organizations ensure that AI helps people do what they already want to do, never manipulates them.

faqs.q: How does AI learn organizational culture?
faqs.a: AI systems learn patterns from the material they are trained on or connected to. When organizations fine-tune models on internal documents or let AI search their knowledge bases, the system absorbs the tone, assumptions, priorities and habits embedded in that material. Because the written record differs from the full culture, AI tends to learn the documented and most frequently expressed version of the organization, including patterns leaders may not intend to repeat.

faqs.q: Can AI reinforce bias from past decisions?
faqs.a: Yes. If historical records reflect biased decisions in areas such as hiring, lending, service or care, an AI system learning from those records can reproduce the same patterns. This is why it matters to audit training and source material, test outputs across different groups and scenarios, and keep humans accountable for consequential decisions. Bias testing should continue after deployment, since patterns can emerge or shift over time.

faqs.q: What should leaders do before deploying AI internally?
faqs.a: Understand what data and documents the system will learn from or retrieve, and remove or flag outdated and unrepresentative material. Capture key expert knowledge and values explicitly. Define where human review is required. Test the system on realistic scenarios, including edge cases. Then plan to measure how the AI changes actual behavior, such as decision quality, customer outcomes and employee practices, rather than tracking usage alone.

insights.title: People Problems Are Business Problems
insights.meta_description: Why performance is behavior, why people problems inside and outside a business are the real business problems, and how behavioral signals make them measurable.
insights.summary: Every business result is the sum of human behavior. Why people problems inside and outside the organization are the real business problems, and how behavioral signals make them measurable.
insights.dek: Revenue, retention, adoption and adherence are not abstractions. They are what happens when people decide to act. Organizations that treat people problems as soft issues miss the source of their results. Organizations that measure behavior can predict and improve them.
key_takeaways: Every business outcome, from conversion to retention to execution, is the accumulated result of specific human behaviors.
People problems exist both inside the business, among leaders and teams, and outside it, among customers, patients and communities.
Treating people problems as soft or unmeasurable leaves organizations guessing about the very behaviors that drive their results.
Behavioral signals in existing data can make people problems visible, predictable and testable, turning guesswork into measurable progress.

sections.heading: Performance is behavior
paragraphs: Look closely at any business result and you will find people deciding to do something. Revenue is customers choosing to buy and choosing to buy again. Growth is prospects noticing, considering and committing. Technology return on investment is employees adopting a system and using it as intended. Health outcomes depend on patients following a care plan and clinicians following evidence. Strategy depends on leaders making sound decisions and teams executing them. Underneath every financial statement is a vast number of individual human actions, taken or not taken, at specific moments. Performance is behavior. That sentence is not a slogan. It is a description of how results are produced, and it has practical consequences for how organizations should be managed.

Yet most organizations are not managed this way. They measure outcomes in great detail and the behaviors that produce those outcomes barely at all. Quarterly reports describe what happened to revenue, churn and engagement, but say little about which behaviors moved and why. Strategies set targets for results without specifying the human actions required to reach them. When results disappoint, organizations reach for familiar levers, such as pricing, headcount, features and campaigns, without diagnosing the behavior that actually failed to occur. The consequence is predictable: expensive interventions aimed at the wrong problem, and a persistent sense that people are hard to understand and harder to predict.

sections.heading: The people problems inside the business
paragraphs: Inside organizations, the most consequential problems are often people problems wearing other labels. A stalled strategy is frequently a leadership alignment problem: senior leaders agree in the meeting and behave differently afterward. A failed technology rollout is usually an adoption problem: the system works, but people do not change their routines to use it. Slow execution often traces to decision-making habits, unclear ownership or teams where it is not safe to raise problems early. High turnover reflects how people experience their managers and their work. These are described as soft issues, discussed in offsites and handed to human resources. In reality, they determine whether the organization can do what its strategy requires.

Treating these problems as soft has a cost. It implies they cannot be measured, so they are managed by anecdote and intuition. It implies they are secondary to hard operational and financial problems, so they receive attention only when they become crises. And it separates them from the analytics capabilities organizations already have. The behavior of leaders and teams leaves traces in calendars, decision records, project histories, survey responses, communication patterns and operational data. Those traces, interpreted carefully and ethically, can show where alignment is breaking down, where adoption is stalling and where teams are struggling, long before results confirm it.

sections.heading: The people problems outside the business
paragraphs: Outside the organization, the people are customers, users, patients, members, students and communities, and their behavior determines nearly every external result. A customer who abandons an application, a user who never activates a feature, a patient who stops taking a medication, a member who lets a membership lapse, a student who disengages: each is a behavior with causes that can be understood. Organizations usually describe these outcomes in aggregate, as conversion rates, churn or nonadherence, which hides the individual moments where people decided not to continue. Those moments are where the real problem lives, and they are rarely where the organization has been looking.
bullets: Customers: conversion, cross-sell, repeat purchase and recommendation are all decisions made at specific moments.
Users: adoption depends on whether a product makes the right behavior easy and rewarding.
Patients: adherence and engagement depend on motivation, ability and prompts in daily life.
Members and students: participation reflects belonging, relevance and the effort required to stay involved.
Communities: public health and social outcomes depend on norms, trust and access.

sections.heading: Why people problems seem unmeasurable, and why they are not
paragraphs: People problems seem unmeasurable for understandable reasons. Behavior is complex and influenced by many factors. The relevant data is often scattered across systems that were never integrated: a customer relationship platform, a billing system, a support queue, a mobile app, an electronic health record, an engagement survey. Each system shows a fragment, and no one sees the whole journey. Where data is missing, assumptions quietly fill the gaps. Teams come to believe they know why customers leave or why employees disengage, and those beliefs shape strategy without ever being tested. Over time, the untested assumptions become the organization's model of human behavior, and nobody remembers they were assumptions at all.

The good news is that behavior leaves signals. Every click, visit, call, login, refill, renewal, response and decision is a behavioral data point. When those signals are connected across the full journey, patterns emerge. A few key behavioral moments, or conversion points, usually account for most of the difference between people who reach the desired outcome and people who do not. People cluster into behavioral types, defined by what they do rather than who they are demographically, and those types respond differently to interventions. Psychometrically sound surveys add the why behind the what. Together, these signals make people problems measurable, predictable and, crucially, testable.

sections.heading: From signals to measurable change
paragraphs: Measurement is only the beginning. The goal is to change behavior in ways that improve outcomes, and to know with confidence that the change worked. That requires a disciplined sequence. First, observe how people actually behave, through qualitative research and journey mapping, so that data is interpreted in context. Second, find the signals that predict outcomes and turn them into predictive, behavior-based KPIs that move before results do. Third, design interventions grounded in behavioral science, whether a redesigned onboarding flow, a better-timed message, a coaching plan or a new team routine. Fourth, test those interventions with experiments, A/B tests or pilots. Fifth, scale what works and build the leadership capability to sustain it.

This approach replaces the most expensive guess in business, the guess about how people will behave, with evidence. It also changes the conversation between functions. When marketing, operations, product, clinical and people teams share a behavioral view of the outcome, they stop arguing from intuition and start testing hypotheses together. The work stays ethical when it is grounded in a simple principle: behavioral science should help people do what they already want to do. Customers want products that work. Patients want to get well. Employees want to do good work. Designing for those goals is both the right thing to do and the most reliable way to improve performance.

sections.heading: How Datalidy puts this into practice
paragraphs: The conviction that people problems are business problems is the foundation of Datalidy's work. Our Behavioral Signals Design methodology starts from the outcome that matters, maps the journey and the data around it, identifies the conversion points and behavioral types that drive results, surfaces untested assumptions and defines predictive KPIs with clear tests to improve them. Our engagements follow five phases: Observe, Signal, Design, Test and Scale. We apply them to customers, users and patients outside the organization, and to leaders and teams inside it, through behavioral design, experimentation and executive and team coaching. Read the signals. Design the behavior. Measure what matters.

faqs.q: What does performance is behavior mean?
faqs.a: It means that every business result is produced by people taking or not taking specific actions. Revenue reflects purchasing behavior, adoption reflects usage behavior, health outcomes reflect patient and clinician behavior, and execution reflects leadership and team behavior. Managing performance well therefore requires understanding, measuring and influencing those behaviors directly, rather than tracking only the outcomes they eventually produce.

faqs.q: How can people problems be measured?
faqs.a: People problems leave behavioral signals in data organizations already collect: transactions, usage logs, service records, health data, survey responses and operational systems. Connecting these signals across the full journey reveals the key behavioral moments and behavioral types that drive outcomes. Well-designed surveys add insight into motivation and experience. Together they allow organizations to define predictive KPIs and test interventions rather than relying on assumptions.

faqs.q: Why do organizations treat people problems as soft issues?
faqs.a: Partly because behavior is complex, and partly because the relevant data is scattered across systems that were never integrated, so no one sees the whole picture. When something cannot easily be measured, it tends to be treated as secondary. Recognizing that behavior leaves measurable signals changes this. People problems become as analyzable and testable as operational or financial ones, and often more decisive.
